intro: A deviation along a tightly constrained direction matters more than the same deviation along a variable direction. Precision-weighted geometry captures that distinction.
task: Return squared Mahalanobis distances using a supplied symmetric positive-definite precision matrix.
requirements: points is an (n,d) matrix, center is a length-d vector, and precision is a (d,d) matrix.
precision must be symmetric within 1e-10 and have every eigenvalue at least 1e-8. Return one value (point-center).T@precision@(point-center) per row.
The output is squared distance, without a square root. A precision matrix is the inverse covariance; do not invert it again.

Use real finite numeric inputs with magnitude at most 1e6, excluding booleans. Vectors have length 1..128 and matrix axes have length 1..128 unless a tighter bound is stated. Leave all inputs unchanged; raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Find the structure
hints.body: Subtract the center from each point, then apply the precision matrix in the quadratic form.

hints.title: Build the calculation
hints.body: Precision already describes inverse covariance, so no additional inversion belongs inside this scoring operation.

explanation: A quadratic form combines scale and cross-coordinate relationships. For diagonal precision, the formula becomes a weighted sum of squared coordinate differences.
Using a supplied precision avoids repeatedly solving or inverting a covariance inside a scoring loop. The squared convention is useful in Gaussian log densities and should remain explicit.
